# Waves in Stratified Atmospheres {#sec-strat}

## Waves in Isothermal Atmospheres

Consider a stratified, static, isothermal atmosphere. We assume constant acceleration $g$ in the negative $z$ direction. The hydrostatic equilibrium equations are
$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g, &{}\qquad{} && p = a^2 \rho,
\end{alignedat}
$$ {#eq-strat-1}
where $a = \sqrt{\frac{kT}{\mu}}$ is the isothermal sound speed.

Combining these two we find
$$
\partial_z \rho_0 = - \frac{g}{a ^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 =
\tilde{\rho} e^{- z / H} .
$$ {#eq-strat-2}
$H = a^2 / g$ is called the scale-high of the atmosphere and has units of a length.

We want to study the propagation of waves in this atmosphere. The continuity equation still gives
$$
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}.
$$ {#eq-strat-3}
and the velocity perturbation is
$$
\vb{v}' = \delta \vb{v}- (\vb{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \vb{v}_0 =
\delta \vb{v}= \frac{\dd \vb{\xi}}{\dd t} = \frac{\partial
\vb{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\vb{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \vb{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \vb{\xi}}{\partial t} .
$$ {#eq-strat-4}
The sound speed is given by
$$
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma a^2 .
$$ {#eq-strat-5}
Which implies that $\delta p = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho$ for adiabatic perturbations. However,
$$
p' \overset{!}{=} \Gamma a^2 \rho',
$$ {#eq-strat-6}
instead we have
$$
\delta p = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow (p' +\vb{\xi} \cdot
\nabla p_0) = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow p' = \Gamma a^2 \delta
\rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z .
$$ {#eq-strat-eulerian-pressure}
The momentum equation reads
$$
\rho \frac{\dd \vb{v}}{\dd t} = - \nabla p - g \rho
\hat{\vb{z}} .
$$ {#eq-strat-8}
Setting $\vb{v}=\vb{v}'$, $p = p_0 + p'$, and $\rho = \rho_0 + \rho'$ yields
$$
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \nabla p_0 - g
\rho_0  \hat{\vb{z}} - \nabla p' - g \rho'  \hat{\vb{z}} +
\operatorname{HOT} .
$$ {#eq-strat-9}
The first two terms on the RHS cancel out. Dropping the higher order terms we find
$$
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \Gamma a^2 \nabla
\delta \rho + g \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \hat{\vb{z}} - g \rho_0 \nabla
\xi_z - g \left( \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \right)
\hat{\vb{z}},
$$ {#eq-strat-euler-in-progress}
where we have used @eq-strat-eulerian-pressure and
$$
\rho' = \delta \rho - (\vb{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \rho_0 = \delta r +
\frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
$$ {#eq-strat-11}
The second and last term on the RHS of @eq-strat-euler-in-progress cancel out leaving
$$
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \Gamma a^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\vb{z}} .
$$ {#eq-strat-12}
Using the fact that
$$
\nabla \delta \rho = \nabla (- \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}) = - \rho_0
\nabla \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}- \nabla \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}= -
\rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}+ \frac{\rho_0}{H} \nabla \cdot
\vb{\xi} \hat{\vb{z}},
$$ {#eq-strat-13}
We obtain
$$
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = + \Gamma a^2 \rho_0
\nabla \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}- \rho_0 \Gamma g \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}
\hat{\vb{z}} - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z + g \rho_0 \nabla \cdot
\vb{\xi} \hat{\vb{z}} .
$$ {#eq-strat-14}
This can be simplified to
$$
\boxed{ \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = c_s^2  \left(
\nabla \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}- \frac{a^2}{c_s^2}  \frac{1}{H} \nabla
\xi_z \right) - \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}
\hat{\vb{z}} .}
$$ {#eq-strat-oscillation-stratified}
We are going to analyze the consequences of this equation shortly. Before we do that, we show that this equation reduces to Eq. (6.31) of @clarke2007 in the limit of vertical oscillations in the $z$ direction. To do that, we take the divergence of @eq-strat-oscillation-stratified to obtain
$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} &{}={} && c_s^2  \left( \nabla^2
\delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} \right) + g \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z -
\frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H}  \left( \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta
\rho}{H} \right) \\
&{}={} && c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho - \frac{c_s^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho +
\frac{a^2}{H} \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z + \frac{a^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho +
a^2  \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} .
\end{alignedat}
$$ {#eq-strat-16}
Assuming that $\delta \rho = \delta \rho (t, z)$ and $\vb{\xi}= \xi_z \hat{\vb{z}}$, we obtain,
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2  \frac{\partial^2 \delta
\rho}{\partial z^2} - \frac{c_s^2}{H}  \frac{\partial \delta \rho}{\partial
z} = 0,
$$ {#eq-strat-oscillation-book}
where we have used the fact that
$$
\nabla^2 \xi_z = \partial_z^2 \xi_z = \partial_z  \left( - \frac{\delta
\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = - \frac{\partial_z \delta \rho}{\rho_0} -
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0 H} .
$$ {#eq-strat-18}
@eq-strat-oscillation-book is identical to Eq. (6.31) of @clarke2007. It describes the propagation of density modes in a stratified atmosphere, but neglects an entirely different class of modes that have $\vb{\xi}$ in the z-direction, but propagate in the xy-plane.

As before, we look for traveling wave solutions
$$
\vb{\xi}=\vb{\eta}e^{\ii (\vb{k} \cdot \vb{x}- \omega t)}
.
$$ {#eq-strat-19}
Inserting this into @eq-strat-oscillation-stratified we obtain
$$
\boxed{\omega^2 \vb{\eta}= c_s^2  \left( \vb{k} \cdot
\vb{\eta}+ \ii \frac{a^2}{c_s^2}  \frac{1}{H} \eta_z \right)
\vb{k}+ \ii \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} \vb{k} \cdot \vb{\eta}
\hat{\vb{z}} .}
$$ {#eq-strat-20}

- In the limit of $H \gg a^2 k / \omega^2$, that is, in the limit in which the wavelength of perturbations is much smaller than the scale height of the atmosphere, we recover the dispersion relation for waves in a homogeneous medium, namely $\omega^2 = c_s k^2$, as expected.

- Purely horizontal waves, with $\vb{\eta}, \vb{k} \perp \hat{\vb{z}}$ cannot satisfy the dispersion relation, unless $c_s = a$, that is for isothermal as opposed to adiabatic perturbations. Physically this means that density fluctuations become buoyant, so they acquire a $k_z \neq 0$ component in their wave vector.

- Waves with $\vb{\eta} \parallel \vb{k} \parallel \hat{\vb{z}}$ satisfy the dispersion relation simplifies to
  $$
  \omega^2 = c_s^2  \left( k^2 + \ii \frac{1}{H} k \right)
  \Longrightarrow k_{1, 2} = - \frac{\ii}{2 H} \pm \sqrt{\left(
  \frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{1}{2 H} \right)^2} .
  $$ {#eq-strat-dispersion-relation-stratified}
  These are the so called pressure or p-modes of the atmosphere. They are the generalization of sound waves.

  - If $H \gg \frac{c_s}{\omega}$, then the dispersion relation for p-modes can be approximated as:
    $$
    k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\ii}{2 H} \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
    $$ {#eq-strat-22}
    In this case the displacement grows exponentially with height:
    $$
    \xi_z = \eta_z e^{\ii (\vb{k} \cdot \vb{x}- \omega t)} =
    \eta_z \exp \left[ \ii \omega \left( \pm \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right)
    \right] \exp \left( \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
    $$ {#eq-strat-xiz-stratified-atmosphere}
    This means that waves propagating vertically along an isothermal atmosphere eventually become nonlinear and will experience wave-breaking. Note that the density fluctuation remains finite:
    $$
    \delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \vb{\xi}= - \tilde{\rho} \eta_z
    \left( \frac{\ii \omega}{c_s} + \frac{1}{2 H} \right) \exp \left[
    \ii \omega \left( \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left( -
    \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
    $$ {#eq-strat-24}

  - If $H \ll \frac{c_s}{\omega}$, then the solution describes one of two global oscillation modes of the atmosphere:
    $$
    k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\ii}{H}, 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
    [\xi_z]_{1, 2} = \eta  e^{\ii \omega t}, \eta_z e^{z / H} e^{\ii
    \omega t} .
    $$ {#eq-strat-25}

- Let us now consider the case of perturbations with horizontal displacement. We can align the $x$-axis with $\vb{\eta}$, meaning that $\vb{\eta}= \eta \hat{\vb{x}}$. In this case, the dispersion relation becomes
  $$
  \omega^2 \eta \hat{\vb{x}} = c_s^2  (k_x \eta) \vb{k}+ \ii
  \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} k_x \eta \hat{\vb{z}} .
  $$ {#eq-strat-g-modes}
  This means that there are two components of $\vb{k}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc} k_x & 0 & k_z \end{array}\right)$. The x-component of @eq-strat-g-modes is
  $$
  \omega^2 = c_s^2 k_x^2 \Longrightarrow k_x = \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
  $$ {#eq-strat-27}
  The $z$-component of @eq-strat-g-modes is
  $$
  k_z = - \ii \left( 1 - \frac{a^2}{c_s^2} \right)  \frac{1}{H} .
  $$ {#eq-strat-28}
  The corresponding displacement is
  $$
  \vb{\xi} (t, \vb{x}) = \eta \exp \left[ \ii \omega \left( \pm
  \frac{x}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left[ \left( 1 - \frac{a^2}{c_s^2}
  \right)  \frac{z}{H} \right]  \hat{\vb{x}} .
  $$ {#eq-strat-29}
  Note that, as in the previous case, the density fluctuations $\delta \rho$ remain finite. These are the so called (internal) gravity-modes or g-modes of the atmosphere. In the limit in which $c_s \rightarrow a$, that is $\Gamma \rightarrow 1$ (isothermal perturbations), these type of waves reduce to horizontal sound waves.

## In-class worksheet {#sec-strat-worksheet}

We consider small disturbances in a plane parallel, isothermal atmosphere. We will assume $z$ to be the vertical direction and $g$ to be the gravitational acceleration, assumed to be constant and towards the negative $z$ direction. Let $a = \sqrt{k_B T / \mu}$ be the isothermal sound speed.

1.  Show that the static background density $\rho_0$ satisfies
    $$
    \rho_0 (z) = \tilde{\rho} e^{- z / H},
    $$ {#eq-strat-ws1}
    where $H = a^2 / g$ is the scale height of the atmosphere.

2.  Let $\delta \rho$ and $\rho'$ be the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations of the density. Show that
    $$
    \rho' = \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
    $$ {#eq-strat-ws2}

3.  Let $p'$ be the Eulerian pressure perturbation. Show that
    $$
    p' = c_s^2 \delta \rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z,
    $$ {#eq-strat-ws3}
    where $c_s^2 = \Gamma a^2$ is the square of the sound speed and $\xi_z$ is the $z$-component of the displacement.

4.  Use the results from the previous two points to show that
    $$
    \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \vb{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
    \delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\vb{z}} .
    $$ {#eq-strat-ws4}

## Exercises {#sec-strat-exercises}

::: {#exr-strat-polytropic}
## Waves in a polytropic atmosphere

An isentropic atmosphere sits in a uniform gravitational field $g$, with pressure $p_0 = A \rho_0^{1 + 1/n}$ and $A$ constant. Let $x$ be the depth below the top of the atmosphere, and suppose that the unperturbed density is $\rho_0 = (kx)^n$ with $k$ constant.

1.  Show that hydrostatic equilibrium requires $g = Ak (1 + n)$.

2.  Perturb the atmosphere with a small vertical velocity $u$, taken positive upward, together with adiabatic perturbations $p' \ll p_0$ of the pressure and $\rho' \ll \rho_0$ of the density. Show that $p' = (gx / n) \rho'$.

3.  Show that the linearized continuity and momentum equations are
    $$
    \frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t} - u \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} - \rho_0 \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0
    $$ {#eq-strat-poly-continuity}
    and
    $$
    \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right) g - \frac{g}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} = 0.
    $$ {#eq-strat-poly-momentum}

4.  For $n = 1/2$, combine these equations to show that
    $$
    \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = 2 gx \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + 3 g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} .
    $$ {#eq-strat-poly-wave}

5.  Look for solutions $u (t, x) = u_1 (x) e^{\ii \omega t}$ and change variable to $\tau = (2 x / g)^{1/2}$. Show that @eq-strat-poly-wave becomes
    $$
    \frac{1}{\tau} \frac{\dd^2}{\dd \tau^2} (\tau u_1) + \omega^2 u_1 = 0.
    $$ {#eq-strat-poly-tau}
    Find the solution that stays finite at $x = 0$ and interpret it physically.

Adapted from @clarke2007, Problem 22.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
::: {.solution}
1.  In hydrostatic equilibrium
    $$
    \nabla p = \rho \vb{g} \Longrightarrow A \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n}
    \right) \rho_0^{1 / n} \nabla \rho_0 = - \rho_0 g \hat{\vb{x}} .
    $$
    The gradient of the density is
    $$
    \nabla \rho_0 = - nk^n x^{n - 1}  \hat{\vb{x}} = - \frac{n}{x} \rho_0
    \hat{\vb{x}} .
    $$
    Inserting this into the previous equation, we find
    $$
    g = Ak (1 + n) .
    $$

2.  The Eulerian pressure perturbation is
    $$
    p' = \delta p - (\vb{\xi} \cdot \nabla) p_0 = \delta p - \xi
    \partial_x p_0 .
    $$
    The first component is
    $$
    \delta p = \left( \frac{\dd p}{\dd \rho} \right) \delta \rho = A
    \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right) \rho_0^{1 / n} \delta \rho = \frac{1}{n}
    [A (1 + n) k] x \delta \rho = \frac{gx}{n} \delta \rho .
    $$
    The second component of the pressure perturbation can be found from the condition of hydrostatic equilibrium: $\partial_x p_0 = \rho_0 g$. This can be written in terms of $\partial_x \rho_0$, because
    $$
    \partial_x \rho_0 = nk^n x^{n - 1} = \frac{n}{x} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow
    \partial_x p_0 = \frac{xg}{n} \partial_x \rho_0 .
    $$
    Putting everything together, we find
    $$
    p' = \frac{gx}{n}  (\delta \rho - \xi \partial_x \rho_0) = \frac{gx}{n}
    \rho' .
    $$

3.  The continuity equation reads (note that $x$ decreases upwards, while $u$ is taken to be positive upwards)
    $$
    0 = \frac{\partial (\rho_0 + \rho')}{\partial t} -
    \frac{\partial}{\partial x}  [u (\rho_0 + \rho')] = \frac{\partial
    \rho'}{\partial t} - u \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} - \rho_0
    \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \operatorname{HOT} .
    $$
    The momentum equation reads
    $$
    \begin{alignedat}{2}
    - \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} &{}={} && \frac{1}{\rho_0 + \rho'}  (-
    \partial_x p_0 + \rho_0 g - \partial_x p' + \rho' g) \\
    &{}={} && \frac{1}{\rho_0 + \rho'}  (- \partial_x p' + \rho' g) \\
    &{}={} && \frac{1}{\rho_0}  \left( 1 - \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right)  \left[ -
    \frac{g}{n}  \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} + \rho' g \right] +
    \operatorname{HOT} .
    \end{alignedat}
    $$
    Rearranging terms and dropping all higher order terms, we find
    $$
    \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right) g -
    \frac{g}{n \rho_0}  \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} = 0.
    $$

4.  We can take one more time derivative of the velocity equation to obtain
    $$
    \begin{alignedat}{2}
    \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} &{}={} && - \frac{g}{\rho_0}  \frac{\partial
    \rho'}{\partial t} + \frac{g}{n \rho_0}  \frac{\partial}{\partial x}
    \left[ x \frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t} \right] \\
    &{}={} && - \frac{g}{\rho_0}  \left( u \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} +
    \rho_0  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right) + \frac{g}{n \rho_0}  \left(
    u \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} + \rho_0  \frac{\partial u}{\partial
    x} \right) + \frac{g x}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}  \left( u
    \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} + \rho_0  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}
    \right) \\
    &{}={} && - \frac{g}{\rho_0}  \left( u \frac{n \rho_0}{x} + \rho_0
    \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right) + \frac{g}{n \rho_0}  \left( u
    \frac{n \rho_0}{x} + \rho_0  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right) +
    \frac{g x}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}  \left( u \frac{n
    \rho_0}{x} + \rho_0  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right) \\
    &{}={} && \frac{gu}{x}  (1 - n) + g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \left(
    \frac{1}{n} - 1 \right) + \frac{g x}{n \rho_0}  \left( \frac{n \rho_0}{x}
    \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{un}{x}  \frac{n \rho_0}{x} -
    \frac{un \rho_0}{x^2} + \frac{n \rho_0}{x}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}
    + \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \right) \\
    &{}={} && \frac{gu}{x}  (1 - n) + g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \left(
    \frac{1}{n} - 1 \right) + g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{gu}{x}
    (n - 1) + g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{gx}{n}  \frac{\partial^2
    u}{\partial x^2} \\
    &{}={} && g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}  \left( \frac{1}{n} + 1 \right) +
    \frac{gx}{n}  \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} .
    \end{alignedat}
    $$
    So for $n = 1 / 2$, we obtain
    $$
    \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = 2 gx \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial
    x^2} + 3 g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} .
    $$

5.  We can convert the partial derivative w.r.t. $x$ to one w.r.t. $\tau$ using the chain rule
    $$
    \frac{\partial}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial \tau}{\partial x}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \tau} = \frac{1}{g \tau}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \tau} .
    $$
    Accordingly the velocity equation becomes[^strat-1]
    $$
    \begin{alignedat}{2}
    \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} &{}={} && \tau \frac{\partial}{\partial
    \tau}  \left( \frac{1}{\tau}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \right) +
    \frac{3}{\tau}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \\
    &{}={} && - \frac{1}{\tau}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} +
    \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \tau^2} + \frac{3}{\tau}  \frac{\partial
    u}{\partial \tau} \\
    &{}={} && \frac{1}{\tau}  \frac{\partial^2 (\tau u)}{\partial \tau^2} .
    \end{alignedat}
    $$
    Setting $u (t, \tau) = u_1 (\tau) e^{\ii \omega t}$, we obtain
    $$
    \frac{1}{\tau}  \frac{\dd^2}{\dd \tau^2} (\tau u_1) + \omega^2 u_1
    = 0.
    $$
    To solve this equation, we first expand out the derivative using the product rule to find
    $$
    \frac{\dd^2 u_1}{\dd \tau^2} + \frac{2}{\tau}  \frac{\dd
    u_1}{\dd \tau} + \omega^2 u_1 = 0 \Longrightarrow \tau^2
    \frac{\dd^2 u_1}{\dd \tau^2} + 2 \tau \frac{\dd u_1}{\dd
    \tau} + \omega^2 \tau^2 u_1 = 0
    $$
    We make one more change of variable
    $$
    \begin{alignedat}{2}
    y = \omega \tau, &{}\qquad{} && \frac{\dd}{\dd \tau} = \omega
    \frac{\dd}{\dd y} .
    \end{alignedat}
    $$
    With this definition, the differential equation becomes
    $$
    y^2  \frac{\dd^2 u_1}{\dd y^2} + 2 y \frac{\dd u_1}{\dd y} +
    y^2 u_1 = 0.
    $$
    This is a spherical Bessel equation of order 0, a solution is:
    $$
    j_0 (y) = \frac{\sin y}{y} \Longrightarrow u_1 (\tau) = \frac{\sin
    (\omega \tau)}{\omega \tau} \Longrightarrow u_1 (x) = \frac{\sin [\omega
    (2 x / g)^{1 / 2}]}{\omega (2 x / g)^{1 / 2}} .
    $$
    These are damped sinusoidal waves, with amplitude $\propto \hspace{0.25em} 1 / \sqrt{x}$.

[^strat-1]: Note that $x = g \tau^2 / 2$
:::
:::
